# Owned-base circuit constraints and their physical Schur cost

This note adds second jets and constrained quadratic cap costs to the archived exact shared-original and finite-ownership equations in `candidate 004e194a6aeb29ff`. It does not require one group to cover every fiber. Every original cap has one parameter tuple, even if several groups use it.

The result is a finite-dimensional necessary condition, with precise sufficient regularity for integrating strict jets. A two-group actual triangle example gives a nonzero ONE-SIDED ownership cost: zero in one parity-neutral direction, positive in its reverse. No universal parity bound or OC descent theorem is asserted.

## 1. Actual groups, original caps, and finite ownership

Let P be the finite complete integer projection of a compatible positive-fiber body. Fix a finite list of ORIGINAL nonvertical caps

    H_j={a_j.z+u_j.x-t_j>=0}, u_j!=0.

A group g uses a subset J_g of this same list and has an actual interior source

    Y_g=(z_g,x_g), z_g in P.

Assume every cap of that group passes through Y_g, and choose positive normalized continuous-dependence weights rho_gj satisfying

    a_j.z_g+u_j.x_g-t_j=0, j in J_g,
    sum_(j in J_g) rho_gj=1,
    sum_(j in J_g) rho_gj u_j=0.                         (1)

The cover weights rho are NOT the objective/cap-budget stress multipliers used later. Define

    b_g=sum_(j in J_g) rho_gj a_j,
    ell_g(z)=b_g.(z-z_g).                              (2)

The positive weighted sum of the group's actual margins at (z,x) is ell_g(z), independent of x. Thus ell_g(z)>=0 implies that the group covers the whole continuous fiber space over z. For a minimal full-rank circuit of d+1 normals, this is also necessary: the margin map has image the affine d-plane with that weighted sum, which contains a point with all negative margins whenever the sum is negative.

Fix ownership sets Z_g subset P with union P, and require

    ell_g(z)>=0 for z in Z_g.                           (3)

Overlapping ownership is permitted but unnecessary. This is a finite sufficient cover condition, and an exact whole-fiber condition for the indicated minimal circuits. It is not asserted that every feasible cover motion must preserve this assignment. Different assignments can have different local costs.

The linear ownership cone for b_g is

    O_g={b:b.(z-z_g)>=0 for z in Z_g}.

Only its rows tight at the original b_g constrain first velocities. Strict inequalities carry genuine slack and may not be replaced by equalities. In particular a group owning only its source base has no nontrivial projected-drift constraint.

## 2. Exact first and second jets, including shared caps

Consider a C² one-sided actual path. Every integer source base z_g stays fixed; its continuous source x_g may move. Write

    a_j'=A_j, u_j'=U_j, t_j'=T_j, x_g'=X_g,
    a_j''=AA_j, u_j''=UU_j, t_j''=TT_j, x_g''=XX_g,
    rho_gj'=mu_gj, rho_gj''=nu_gj.

Each ORIGINAL cap has the same A,U,T,AA,UU,TT at all its occurrences. One cannot assign a different normal velocity to a shared occurrence. Differentiating (1) gives the exact first equations

    A_j.z_g+U_j.x_g+u_j.X_g-T_j=0,
    sum_j mu_gj=0,
    sum_j(mu_gj u_j+rho_gj U_j)=0,                       (4)

and second equations

    AA_j.z_g+UU_j.x_g+2U_j.X_g+u_j.XX_g-TT_j=0,
    sum_j nu_gj=0,
    sum_j(nu_gj u_j+2mu_gj U_j+rho_gj UU_j)=0.           (5)

Use a local affine normal gauge, for example one nonzero continuous coordinate fixed to one in a suitable chart for each cap. Its first and second gauge equations are linear. If unit normals are used instead, the additional equations are u_j.U_j=0 and u_j.UU_j=-|U_j|²; these terms must not be omitted.

The projected drift jets are

    b_g'=sum_j(mu_gj a_j+rho_gj A_j),
    b_g''=sum_j(nu_gj a_j+2mu_gj A_j+rho_gj AA_j).       (6)

At an owned base with ell_g(z)=0, one-sided feasibility requires

    b_g'.(z-z_g)>=0.                                   (7)

If this first coefficient is zero, it also requires

    b_g''.(z-z_g)>=0.                                  (8)

Strictly positive initial ownership margins impose neither condition. A strictly positive coefficient in (7) needs no second sign restriction. For a two-sided feasible path, every tight row has first coefficient zero, after which its second coefficient must be nonnegative. These are ordinary Taylor expansions of the ACTUAL projected margin, not a frozen-weight approximation.

For a fixed body/source first and second jet and fixed cap/weight first jet, equations (5), (6), and the required inequalities (8) form a finite LINEAR feasibility problem in the cap and weight accelerations. The terms 2U_j.X_g and 2mu_gj U_j or A_j are already prescribed quadratic constants. Finite-dimensional Farkas gives its exact alternative, with multipliers on every tight ownership row and on every shared-through-source equation. No assumed number of independent equations is needed.

These necessary jet equations are not automatically integrable at singular incidence strata. A precise sufficient version is available: if the exact equality map (through-source, balance, normalization, and gauge) has full row rank in the movable normal/weight variables, the implicit function theorem corrects a trial normal/weight path realizing a prescribed jet satisfying (4)–(5) by an o(s²) term to satisfy the equalities exactly, along the prescribed actual C² body/source path. To see the order, the trial equality residual has zero value and first two derivatives, hence is o(s²); solving with a fixed invertible minor gives a correction of the same order. Strict first or, when first is zero, strict second ownership slack then preserves every nontrivial inequality for small positive s. Identically zero rows such as z=z_g are omitted. Positivity of rho and interior membership of the finite actual sources persist under sufficiently small motions. If a nontrivial ownership row has both displayed coefficients zero, higher-order information is still necessary; it cannot be inferred from these jets.

## 3. The physical quadratic cost with active ownership inequalities

Choose any fixed nonnegative objective weights omega_j on original caps, counted ONCE per cap. These may, when justified separately, be cap-budget stress multipliers. They are distinct from the cover weights rho_gj. Let h describe an actual compatible body/source family, and anchor each cap chart at one of its through-source incidences; all other incidences remain equations (4).

Suppose the positive-weight cap functions are C² in an open proper/transverse chamber and each is stationary with respect to all its through-anchor normal variables at the original point. This holds for an actual attaining normal minimum under the stated smoothness. Their weighted cap sum Phi has expansion, for a body velocity v and normal velocity w,

    q(v,w)=v^T A v+2b(v)^T w+w^T K w,
    b(v)=B^T v, K=Phi_(normal,normal).                     (9)

Assume K is positive definite on the retained active normal coordinates. Normal coordinates absent from the weighted objective, including those of slack zero-weight caps, can instead be included among auxiliary variables eta along with the cover-weight velocities. Do not assert this definiteness for flat integer-tilt modes of a positive-weight cap: they may retain a mixed body-normal force and cannot simply be discarded. Formula (11) below is stated only for the positive-definite block after genuinely objective-absent variables are separated. The preceding Schur note proves the unconstrained singular range test; with ownership constraints a singular quadratic must instead be minimized on its actual feasible polyhedron. Those constraints can remove a null direction, so an unconstrained range failure alone is not a claim of unbounded constrained cost.

After substituting the prescribed body/source velocity, all equations (4), gauge equations, and active ownership inequalities (7) have the form

    Rw+S eta=d(v),
    Gw+H eta>=e(v).                                     (10)

The right sides are linear in v. Define the projected feasible normal-velocity set

    W(v)={w:there exists eta satisfying (10)}.

It is a closed polyhedron: elimination of finitely many real variables in a finite linear inequality system yields another finite linear inequality system, with equalities represented by opposite inequalities. It may be empty; emptiness is a genuine first-order obstruction.

If W(v) is nonempty, put w0=-K^(-1)b(v). Completing the square gives the EXACT first-jet constrained quadratic cost

    min_(w in W(v)) q(v,w)
      =v^T A v-b(v)^T K^(-1)b(v)
          +dist_K(w0,W(v))²,                            (11)

where dist_K² means the minimum of (w-w0)^T K(w-w0). The minimum exists and its w is unique because K is positive definite, W(v) is closed and convex, and the squared norm is coercive. At least one auxiliary eta realizing this w exists by the definition of W(v).

This cost retains the full first-order ownership inequalities; it is generally piecewise quadratic in v rather than one quadratic form. A direct finite proof follows from the multiplier equations in Section 4: fix the subset of tight inequalities and positive multipliers, solve the resulting constant-coefficient linear stationarity/equality system, and retain the remaining linear feasibility and sign conditions. Projection eliminates auxiliary variables and gives a polyhedral parameter region. Uniqueness of w makes its value linear on this region, even if the auxiliary variables or multipliers are nonunique. There are only finitely many active subsets, so their regions cover the feasible velocities and the objective is quadratic on each. It bounds the normal part of every actual feasible path with that body/source velocity. It becomes an attained physical reduced Hessian only when the second-jet and integration requirements of Section 2 are also met. No automatic actual path is claimed from the projection alone.

## 4. Exact finite stress at the metric projection

At a minimizing pair (w*,eta*) in (10), there exist unrestricted equality multipliers lambda and nonnegative multipliers tau on the inequalities tight at that pair such that

    K(w*-w0)+R^T lambda-G^T tau=0,
    S^T lambda-H^T tau=0,
    tau_i [G_i w*+H_i eta*-e_i]=0.                       (12)

These equations, primal feasibility, and tau>=0 are also sufficient for optimality. The factor two in the objective gradient has been absorbed into lambda and tau.

For necessity, first-order optimality of the convex squared norm says its gradient is nonnegative on the polyhedral feasible tangent cone. Farkas represents its negative as a linear combination of equality rows plus a nonnegative combination of the negative active inequality rows, giving (12). This argument needs no strict feasible ownership point. For sufficiency, take the inner product of (12) with any feasible displacement and use complementary slackness; the directional derivative is nonnegative. Adding the nonnegative squared displacement term proves global optimality.

If no auxiliary variables are present and ownership is represented by equalities Rw=d, the added cost reduces to

    [d+R K^(-1)b]^T [R K^(-1)R^T]^dagger
                                  [d+R K^(-1)b].           (13)

This follows by the least-norm calculation in the preceding Schur note. Inequalities require selecting the active face, as in (12); silently replacing them all by equalities can strictly overcharge the motion.

The optimization concerns a specified weighted sum of second cap variations. It does NOT imply that every individual active cap budget improves. For such a claim the individual second budget inequalities, body accelerations, and the second incidence/ownership system must all be retained. The omega used in a valid variational dual may also depend on the tested velocity; there is no universal common multiplier claim here.

## 5. Two actual groups with an exact one-sided ownership penalty

Use the actual planar three-fiber family from the preceding Schur note:

    T=conv{(-1,-1),(2,-1),(-1,2)},
    K_j(a)=(1+a j)T, j=-1,0,1.

For sufficiently small |a| it has positive compatible fibers and actual source centroids (j,0). At a=0 the middle centroid has global raw depth 6 and each endpoint centroid has raw depth 2. The all-direction certification and exact normal Hessians are proved in `candidate 0e4cb84a76d46e82`.

Group A is the actual middle critical circuit with cyclic continuous normals

    u1=(1,0), u2=(0,1), u3=(-1,-1).

Allow its cap margins to be

    (u_i+theta_i u_(i+1)).x+alpha_i z.

For the exact finite calculation retain equal cover weights 1/3. Continuous balance is then precisely theta_i=theta. Assign A the bases {-1,0}, NOT the right endpoint. Its owned-base inequalities reduce exactly to

    sum_i alpha_i<=0.                                    (14)

Group B is an actual right-endpoint critical circuit. Keep its three margins

    u_i.x+10(z-1).

At base 1 these are canonical through-centroid caps. At both other bases their traces are strictly empty for all sufficiently small |a|. Thus each B cap has actual mass 2(1+a)² and is genuinely depth-attaining at its endpoint source: exposed-fiber finite isolation makes its mixed depth equal its ordinary own depth. Assign B only the base {1}. Its projected inequality there is the identity zero, so it adds no drift constraint. Its mass remains strictly below the middle budget 6 for small |a|; this is actual budget slack, not discarded source mass.

The two groups cover every assigned continuous fiber space, hence the whole actual mixed set. All three original fibers remain present. At a=0 they are strictly nonheavy, as are all sufficiently close families. No cap is shared between these two groups; the general equations above allow sharing but the example does not invent independent copies of a shared cap.

Within the middle group's common proper vertex chamber, its exact cap masses are

    Phi_i=6+(3/2)theta²/(1-theta)
                  +(2a+alpha_i-a theta)²/(1-theta).       (15)

For a>=0, choose theta=0 and alpha_i=-2a. This satisfies (14), attains all masses 6, and covers the left owned fiber with strict positive projected margin when a>0. Formula (15) proves no lower maximum is possible.

For a<0 and theta in this nearby chart, 2-theta>0 and k=a(2-theta)<0. Under sum alpha_i<=0, the mean of alpha_i+k is at most k<0. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives

    (1/3)sum_i(alpha_i+k)² >= k².

Consequently max Phi_i is at least

    (3/2+a²)(2-theta)²/(1-theta)
      =6+4a²+(3/2+a²)theta²/(1-theta)
      >=6+4a².

Equality is attained at theta=0 and alpha_i=0. The EXACT local-chamber optimum is therefore

    min_(continuous balance and owned bases) max_i Phi_i
          =6+4(a_-)², a_-=max(-a,0).                    (16)

Both displayed optimizers are actual finite cap motions and preserve the required assignments, so no second-jet integration assumption is needed for this example. Group B can remain fixed throughout and keeps its strict budget slack.

## 6. The projection cost, parity, and what the example proves

For the unweighted sum of the three middle cap Hessians, normal coordinates are their three integer tilts and three angular parameters. The integer-tilt block is 2I, and the mixed force along radius velocity A j is (4A,4A,4A). Thus the unconstrained optimum is alpha_i'=-2A. The active ownership row is sum alpha_i'<=0.

If A>=0 that unconstrained normal velocity is feasible, and the added metric-projection cost is zero. If A<0, its projection is alpha_i'=0; the added second-derivative cost is

    24 A².

Equivalently the exact piecewise cost is 24(A_-)², agreeing with (16). The canonical cap-budget multiplier 3/4 changes this to 18(A_-)². Additional linearized continuous-balance equations do not increase this value, because zero angular velocity attains it. Smooth variable positive cover weights have the same first-order ownership row at the original zero integer drift, so the same second-order optimum remains valid when those weights are allowed to vary.

The body velocity rho_j=A j is actual and sums to zero within EACH integer parity class: the odd bases -1 and 1 cancel, and the even base 0 is stationary. Its total-volume second derivative is 18A² in either direction. Thus even on the SAME parity-neutral body line, the exact owned-base cost is zero on one half-line and positive on the other. It cannot be described by a single parity-only quadratic form.

For A>0, the middle cuts have constant mass 6, the endpoint group stays below 6, and their ownership cover is complete. The actual middle depth remains 6 for sufficiently small a by the already certified all-normal minimum. Hence this is a genuine local improvement in the GLOBAL normalized maximum depth as total mass increases, not merely a stationary single-cap calculation. It starts above OC and supplies no below-target contradiction.

Reversing which endpoint is given its own slack group reverses the one-sided penalty. More generally an alternative finite ownership assignment can change the cost. One must optimize or certify an assignment together with the actual original-cap incidences and budgets; it cannot be inferred from a count of parity classes.

## 7. Scope of the new condition

The new ingredient beyond the archived shared-original first-order equations is the full second-jet system, together with the exact constrained physical Schur distance (11) and its finite ownership stress (12). The two-group formula (16) is an actual geometry realization of the inequality-constrained cost, including a slack source group.

No result here proves that every hypothetical below-target body admits an ownership assignment with sufficiently small cost, that all positive source regions are covered by globally deepest groups alone, or that the same original cap can move independently in two groups. Those statements would require additional geometry. All shared planes, second-order ownership inequalities, and individual active cap budgets remain explicit dependencies.
